metadata.file_name: Factors affecting teacher job satisfaction  a causal inference machine learning approach using data from TALIS 2018.pdf
metadata.title: Factors affecting teacher job satisfaction: a causal inference machine learning approach using data

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the English subset of TALIS 2018, which is collected using a stratified two-stage probability sampling design within each country. Each teacher is assigned sampling weights, and the authors state that these sampling weights were fully accounted for in the analysis. They implement this using the Balanced Repeated Replication (BRR) procedure described in the TALIS technical report (OECD, 2019b), which is consistent with replicate-weight variance estimation for complex survey designs. The paper does not report a specific weight variable name in the provided text, but it explicitly indicates that complex survey weights and BRR replicate procedures were used when estimating treatment effects and confidence intervals.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variable is a continuous teacher job satisfaction scale constructed from eight Likert items using confirmatory factor analysis, rather than a PV-based cognitive achievement score. Missing data handling is reported: the authors impute missing responses using missRanger, which substitutes missing values with predictions from other survey responses; however, the paper does not describe multiple imputation and therefore the approach is treated as single imputation for this extraction.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the English subset of TALIS 2018, restricting the full TALIS teacher sample to England only. The analytic sample comprises 2009 primary and 2376 lower secondary teachers (total n=4385). The outcome is teacher job satisfaction measured from eight Likert items and converted into a continuous scale by TALIS organisers; the study also imputes missing values for variables used in the analysis (52 variables with ~8% missing on average) using missRanger rather than deleting cases.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (England subset) teacher job satisfaction scale
main_findings.performance_metrics: Causal inference ML (bartCause/BART) estimated ATEs with 95% confidence intervals: CPD (ATE CI [0.035, 0.309]); Induction (ATE CI [0.107, 0.329]); Team teaching (CI includes 0); Observing (CI includes 0); Part-time contract (ATE CI [-0.388, -0.044]).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (England subset) the study leveraged CPD participation (4+ events), induction programme participation, and part-time contract status (among other treatment indicators) to predict teacher job satisfaction, finding that participation in continual professional development and induction activities had the most positive average treatment effects while part-time contracts had a negative effect. This indicates that school and system leaders should prioritize accessible CPD and induction supports to improve teacher job satisfaction, while reviewing how part-time employment arrangements may contribute to lower satisfaction, though the estimates rely on causal assumptions and observational treatment assignment.

data.outcome_summary: The study applies a causal inference machine learning approach (bartCause using Bayesian Additive Regression Trees, BART) to the English subset of TALIS 2018, analyzing 4,385 teachers (2009 primary; 2376 lower secondary). Teacher job satisfaction is measured from eight Likert items and converted into a continuous scale (mean 12.42, SD 2.28). Using BRR-based complex survey weighting, the authors estimate average treatment effects (ATEs) for binary “treatments” including CPD (≥4 events), induction, observing, team teaching, mentoring, public school employment, class size (30+), out-of-field teaching, and part-time contracts (<90%). CPD shows a positive ATE with 95% CI [0.035, 0.309], induction is the strongest positive effect with CI [0.107, 0.329], and part-time contracts reduce job satisfaction with ATE CI [-0.388, -0.044]. For team teaching and observing, confidence intervals include zero, so effects are imprecisely estimated; the paper also imputes missing covariate responses with missRanger (single imputation), and causal claims depend on ignorability/overlap assumptions.
